## What you just did, as a flowchart and a checklist
:::

```{=html}
<div id="b2-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Time stamps</dt><dd>EIA-930 stamps each hour in UTC at its end; label hours by their start and convert to local time before grouping by day.</dd>
<dt>Range, repeats, physics</dt><dd>Three different checks catch three different faults: a spike, a stuck sensor, and sun at night.</dd>
<dt>Mean or sum</dt><dd>Average power uses the mean; energy uses the sum of hourly MW values (each is that hour's MWh).</dd>
<dt>Duration curve</dt><dd>The year's hours sorted from highest to lowest; for a plant, the area under it over the full box is the capacity factor.</dd>
<dt>Assert</dt><dd>A check that stops the notebook with a message when the data break a rule.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Why one hour of offset matters to a model</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>An hourly model treats value <em>t</em> as the energy of hour <em>t</em>. Shift the stamps by one hour and the solar peak moves an hour, which changes when a battery should charge and what it earns. Days of 23 and 25 hours also break code that assumes 24 rows a day, so keep a time-zone-aware index and let pandas place each hour.</p>
<p>Modeler's note: the lab's notebook is the template for every later lab; upcoming M10 (forecasting) and M14 (learning from data) start from a frame checked like this one.</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>A capacity factor needs a capacity</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<p>A capacity factor is energy divided by (nameplate capacity × hours). EIA-930 reports generation, not capacity, so a real fleet's capacity factor needs a second source, such as EIA's generator inventory (Form EIA-860).</p>
<p>Dividing by the year's best hour instead gives a higher number, because no fleet runs all its turbines at nameplate at once. Prairie Town's farms are defined to reach full output in SPP's best hour, which is why their 52.8% and 23.8% are labelled illustrative. Lesson 5 on the <a href="index.html#lesson-5">course map</a> builds capacity factors from scratch.</p>
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>How the data build filled the gaps, and what it missed</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Repeated wind and solar readings were replaced by the mean of the same hour on up to seven valid days before and after.</li>
<li>Implausible demand hours were replaced by the day-ahead forecast, rescaled to the actual demand around the gap.</li>
<li>From 20 February to 14 March raw solar barely changed between day and night but never repeated exactly, so the repeat rule kept it, and the same-hour fill then drew on those days. The night check finds 64 failing hours in the cleaned file: 15 kept from the raw data and 49 written by the fill. The notebook flags those days and refills them.</li>
</ul>
<p>Upcoming: R4 (data you can defend) turns these choices into a written data note.</p>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

::: {#check .lx-sec}

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="b2-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="day" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Every local day has 24 hours.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. Where clocks change, one spring day has 23 hours and one autumn day has 25; in 2025 in U.S. Central time, 9 March and 2 November.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="summary" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “If the summary statistics look normal, every row is fine.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. 617 MW is a normal solar value, but not at 2 a.m.; repeat and physics checks look at rows and their times, not just at summaries.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cf" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Average wind output divided by the year's best hour is the wind fleet's capacity factor.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. A <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-factor">capacity factor</span> divides by nameplate capacity, which is at least the best hour; that ratio overstates it.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="b2">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="mwh" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">A wind farm's hourly output is 100 MW in every hour of one day. How much <span class="lx-term" data-term="energy">energy</span> did it make that day?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">100 MWh</li><li data-value="b">2,400 MWh</li><li data-value="c">4.2 MW</li><li data-value="d">2,400 MW</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>2,400 MWh: each hourly value is also that hour's MWh, so the day's energy is the sum, 24 × 100.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="sum" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">You resample hourly MW values to months. Which gives each month's energy?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">The mean</li><li data-value="b">The sum</li><li data-value="c">The maximum</li><li data-value="d">The median</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>The sum, in MWh (divide by 1,000 for GWh). The mean gives the month's average power in MW.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::
